label: Show, recital or concert

what_happens.title: What happens at the show
goals: A show has practice, waiting, performing and a bow
The audience is friendly, mostly families
Clapping at the end means well done
what_happens.parentSkill: Explain the order: costume, waiting, stage, perform, bow, hugs.

who_is_there.title: Who is at the show
goals: The teacher or director guides the performers
The audience wants the performers to do well
who_is_there.parentSkill: Tell your child where you will sit and agree a small signal, like touching your nose.

what_i_do.title: What I do on stage
goals: Breathe, look at a friendly face, start
If a mistake happens, keep going
what_i_do.parentSkill: Practise the part in front of toys, then family, then a video call.

if_scared.title: If I get stage fright
goals: Shaky knees and butterflies pass once it starts
Calm tools: breathing, a friendly face, a plan if I freeze
if_scared.parentSkill: Name it and normalise it: 'Lots of performers get butterflies. They go away once you start.'

rehearsal.title: Let's practise the show
goals: Do a home show for toys and family
Practise the walk on, the part and the bow
Practise keeping going after a pretend mistake
rehearsal.parentSkill: Hold a living-room show with toys as the audience and a lamp as the stage light.

steps: Practise the part, song or piece at home
Put on the costume or the special clothes
Wait backstage or in a line with the group
Walk onto the stage when it is time
Perform the part with the group or alone
Meet the family after the show
sensory: bright stage lights that make it hard to see the audience
a quiet, dark room full of people
a costume that feels scratchy or new
a fluttery tummy and shaky knees
music from a piano or speakers
honestyNotes: Mistakes happen in almost every show and the audience rarely notices; never promise it will be perfect. Stage fright is normal. A child can freeze or cry; agree a calm plan with the teacher. Praise courage and effort, not perfection.

questionButtons.text: What if I forget my part?
fallbackAnswer: It happens to lots of performers. Take a breath, and the teacher can whisper a hint.
Then you keep going.

questionButtons.text: What if I make a mistake?
fallbackAnswer: Most people will not even notice. Keep going like nothing happened.
[[GROWNUP]] will be proud of you for being brave.
[[GROWNUP]] will tell you where they will sit.
You can agree a special signal, like touching your nose.

questionButtons.text: Why are the lights so bright?
fallbackAnswer: Stage lights help the audience see you.
They can make it hard to see the audience, and that can help with nerves.
Mostly families and friends.
Everyone in the audience wants you to do well.
Butterflies mean your body is excited and nervous.
They usually get smaller when you start.
If people laugh, it is usually because something is funny or cute, not at you.
You can smile and keep going.
The teacher knows the order and will tell you when to go on.
You wait quietly with your group until then.

questionButtons.text: What if I cry on stage?
fallbackAnswer: If you feel too big a feeling, the teacher will help.
It is okay, and you can try again next time.
Freezing for a moment happens. Breathe out slowly, look at the teacher, and start from the last part.
The audience will wait kindly.

techniques.label: A living-room show
techniques.how: Perform for toys and family at home first.

techniques.label: A special signal
techniques.how: Agree a signal like touching the nose from the audience.

techniques.label: A friendly face
techniques.how: Look at a friendly face or a spot at the back.

techniques.label: Keep going practice
techniques.how: Practise making a mistake on purpose and carrying on.

techniques.label: Practising in pieces
techniques.how: Practise small parts, then join them.

techniques.label: A sip of water
techniques.how: Have water backstage for a dry mouth.

techniques.label: A power pose
techniques.how: Stand tall with hands on hips for a few breaths backstage.

techniques.label: A hint plan
techniques.how: Ask the teacher to whisper a hint if your child forgets.

techniques.label: Smell the flower, blow the candle
techniques.how: Breathe in slowly through the nose and out like blowing a candle.

ritual: One slow breath, then walk on

pain: If something feels uncomfortable in the costume, tell the teacher.
body: Butterflies mean your body is excited.
A sip of water helps a dry mouth.
sensory: The lights are bright. That is normal on a stage.
The clapping is loud because people liked it.
strangers: The audience is on your side.
The teacher will tell you when to go on.
separation: I'll be in the audience. Look for my signal.
I will be clapping the loudest.
safety: If you forget, breathe and keep going.
The teacher can whisper a hint.
social: Your group is doing it with you.
love: I'm proud of you for being brave on stage.

sentences.text: Soon [[CHILD]] will be in a show.
A show is when performers share a song, a dance, a play or music with an audience.
First [[CHILD]] puts on the costume or the special clothes.
Then the group waits backstage, quietly, for their turn.
Before bed, here is a story about a little cricket called Kit.
Kit was going to play a song in the Garden Concert.
First Kit put on a shiny green bow tie.
Then Kit waited behind a big leaf with the other bugs.
The ladybird sang first, then the bees buzzed a tune.
Next it was Kit's turn.
Kit hopped onto the stage, a flat stone under the moonlight.
The fireflies glowed like stage lights.
Kit played chirp, chirp, chirp, the song from practice.
At the end, Kit bowed, and all the garden clapped.
Tomorrow evening, the story goes on.
Next they walk onto the stage, and the lights are bright.
After that, they perform the part they practised.
At the end, everyone bows, and the audience claps.
Last, families meet the performers with hugs.
[[CHILD]] can remember: wait, walk on, perform, bow.

Before a show, the tummy may feel full of butterflies.
The knees may shake, and the mouth may feel dry.
This is called stage fright, and lots of performers feel it, even famous ones.
The feeling is strongest right before going on.
In the story, Kit the cricket felt stage fright.
Kit's legs wobbled, and Kit's mouth felt dry.
Mama Cricket did not say, nothing will go wrong.
Mama said, your body is excited and nervous at the same time.
If you forget, Miss Moth will whisper a hint.
Kit took a sip of dew water.
Then Kit smelled a flower slowly and blew a candle.
When the music began, the wobbles got smaller.
By the end, Kit was having fun.
Mama hugged Kit and said, I am proud of you.
Worried and brave can happen at the same time.
Once the show starts, it usually gets smaller.

It is okay to feel nervous and still do it.

Performances have a running order, so each group knows when they go on.
Stage lights are bright so the audience can see the performers, which means performers often see only darkness.
A dress rehearsal is the practice run with costumes and lights.
Professional performers make small mistakes too and simply keep going.
[[CHILD]] can ask the teacher for the running order to know exactly when the turn comes.
Audiences at school shows are almost all parents and grandparents cheering for someone.
Directors and teachers plan cues, signals that tell performers when to start or move.
Ensemble members support each other on stage; if one forgets, others carry on.
Backstage helpers sort costumes and props.
[[CHILD]] can thank the teacher after the show.
Practising in chunks, then joining them, is how musicians and actors learn long pieces.
Looking just above the audience's heads gives the feeling of eye contact without the nerves.
If words are forgotten, a pause, a breath and the next line usually brings them back.
Recovering from a slip smoothly is a performance skill in itself.
[[CHILD]] can practise one run-through a day in the week before.
Stage fright is the body's alarm system reacting to being watched; it is uncomfortable but harmless.
Slow exhaling tells the nervous system it is safe and calms shaking.
Many performers reframe nerves as excitement because the body feels almost the same.
If [[CHILD]] freezes, a plan helps: breathe, look at the teacher, start again from the last line.
[[CHILD]] can choose a power pose to do backstage.
Running the whole performance at home in the costume removes surprises.
Recording a practice and watching it back shows that small mistakes are hard to spot.
A pre-show routine, like a stretch and a breath, gives the body a calm cue.
Packing water, a hair tie and a snack keeps the waiting easier.
[[CHILD]] can invite a grandparent to a video call for an extra practice audience.
